## The Core Claim

Classical computers require computational resources that scale exponentially with the number of particles being simulated when modeling quantum-mechanical systems, because a quantum system's state space grows exponentially with its degrees of freedom; Feynman proposed (1981) that a computer built from quantum-mechanical components, obeying the same quantum rules as the system being simulated, could in principle simulate quantum systems with resources scaling only polynomially -- the founding proposal of quantum computing. NOTE, disclosed: Feynman's 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics was for quantum electrodynamics, not for this quantum-computation proposal specifically -- the computational insight is real, well-documented, and historically foundational (widely credited as the origin of the field), but is not itself the cited Nobel-winning work -- a real gap in the 'won a Nobel for this' pattern the other cases here share cleanly.
